strengths: The paper addresses an important and relevant NLP problem: making pretrained Transformer LLMs usable on very long contexts with bounded memory and improved inference efficiency.

The proposed architecture is technically plausible and clearly motivated: a gated fixed-size global memory for long-range retention plus FIFO temporary memory for recent detail is a sensible design, and the paper gives reasonably clear equations and implementation-level descriptions.
The empirical scope is broader than a single synthetic benchmark, covering SCROLLS, shorter QA tasks, passkey retrieval, efficiency measurements, and two application-oriented settings.
The results on SCROLLS are encouraging: CoMeT is the strongest efficient method on average and is especially competitive on summarization tasks compared with the fine-tuned full-attention baseline.

The ablations support the intended division of labor between global and temporary memory, and the no-gate result on passkey retrieval provides useful evidence that the gating mechanism is not cosmetic.
The efficiency claims are largely consistent with the architecture: chunk-wise processing with fixed memory should yield linear prefill time and constant memory with respect to input length.
weaknesses: Several central claims are overstated. The paper repeatedly says CoMeT enables arbitrarily long sequences, but the strongest evidence is mainly passkey retrieval up to 1M tokens; this does not establish robust arbitrary-length reasoning or comprehension.

The 1M-token result is on a synthetic passkey task after training on the same task family, so it is weak evidence for general long-range reasoning. More diverse needle variants, multi-needle retrieval, adversarial distractors, and long-context reasoning benchmarks would be needed to support the broader claim.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The abstract says code is available but the link is blank in the manuscript, and key real-world datasets are proprietary or expert-curated without enough detail for independent replication.

The baseline comparison leaves some fairness questions. It is not always clear whether all baselines received equally careful tuning, whether reported compression and finite-state methods are implemented under optimal settings, or how sensitive conclusions are to memory budget and chunk size.
The paper lacks statistical uncertainty, multiple seeds, or significance analysis, despite small margins on some benchmarks and heterogeneous task metrics.

The real-world UQA and agent experiments are interesting but hard to audit: UQA uses private data and LLM-as-judge evaluation, while the agent setting compares only CoMeT and full attention because other methods are said to be infeasible.

The method is incremental in ingredients: recurrent memory, gated updates, memory tokens, compression tokens, and FIFO buffers all have precedents. The contribution is a useful integration, but the novelty is not as strong as the presentation suggests.

Some evaluation choices weaken the main-conference case: SCROLLS contexts are mostly far shorter than the headline 1M setting, and the paper does not test modern long-context suites or tasks requiring compositional reasoning over very distant evidence.

strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP systems problem: adapting pretrained Transformer LLMs to long-context processing with bounded memory and improved inference efficiency.

The proposed design is conceptually coherent: a gated global recurrent memory for long-range retention plus a FIFO temporary memory for recent detail is a reasonable architecture, and the ablations on passkey retrieval support the intended roles of these components.

The manuscript includes a range of evaluations beyond a single benchmark, including SCROLLS, short-context QA sanity checks, synthetic 1M-token retrieval, and efficiency measurements for prefill/decode latency and memory.
The method is described at a high level clearly enough to understand the main recurrence, gating, and memory-token mechanisms.
weaknesses: The central claims are overstated relative to the evidence. Claims such as arbitrarily long processing, accurate 1M-token retrieval, and practical real-world utility rely heavily on a synthetic passkey task and fixed-memory assumptions; they do not establish robust long-context reasoning at extreme lengths.

Reproducibility is weak. The abstract says code is available but no URL is provided, key datasets are proprietary or only loosely described, and important training/inference details for the pipeline parallelism, memory update implementation, and baseline tuning are missing.

The empirical comparison is not fully convincing. Several baselines appear much weaker than expected, the fairness of training and hyperparameter tuning across efficient methods is unclear, and there are no confidence intervals, variance estimates, or statistical tests.

The SCROLLS results are mixed: CoMeT is best among the efficient methods on average, but remains below fine-tuned full attention overall and is notably weak on some QA/NLI tasks. The paper’s narrative emphasizes summarization wins while under-discussing these failures.

The real-world evaluations are hard to assess. UQA is proprietary and judged with an LLM, while the agent benchmark reports only a narrow comparison where most efficient baselines are omitted because training is inconvenient. This limits both soundness and reproducibility.

The novelty is incremental. The paper combines known ingredients from recurrent memory Transformers, compression tokens, gated recurrent updates, and sliding/FIFO memories, but does not sharply distinguish its contribution from closely related memory Transformer systems beyond empirical claims.

The layer-level pipeline parallelism is underspecified and not rigorously evaluated. The claimed 2.7x speedup is not supported with enough detail about hardware utilization, communication cost, scaling curves, or comparison to established pipeline/context parallel methods.

The passkey extrapolation experiment is potentially misleading because the model is explicitly fine-tuned on the same synthetic retrieval pattern. It is not clear that success transfers to semantically richer retrieval, multi-hop reasoning, or adversarial long-context settings.

The limitations section is superficial and does not address the main concerns: baseline fairness, private data, missing code link, narrow extreme-length evaluation, and the gap between synthetic retrieval and real long-context understanding.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and highly relevant NLP problem: enabling pretrained Transformer LLMs to process very long contexts with bounded memory and practical latency.

The proposed CoMeT architecture is technically sensible: combining a gated global recurrent memory with a FIFO temporary memory directly targets the complementary needs of long-range retention and recent-context fidelity.
The empirical evaluation is fairly broad, covering SCROLLS, shorter QA tasks, synthetic passkey retrieval up to 1M tokens, efficiency measurements, and two application-oriented settings.

Ablations provide useful support for the architectural choices: temporary memory appears important for in-domain benchmark performance, while gated global memory is critical for extreme length extrapolation in passkey retrieval.
The efficiency results are compelling in spirit, showing constant memory behavior and stable decoding latency where full attention becomes impractical.
The paper is generally clear, well structured, and situated within relevant work on recurrent Transformers, context compression, and efficient long-context modeling.
weaknesses: The strongest claims, especially 'arbitrarily long sequences' and 1M-token robustness, rely heavily on synthetic passkey retrieval; this does not fully establish long-range reasoning or faithful use of distributed evidence over million-token contexts.
Reproducibility is weakened by missing or unclear release details: the abstract says code is available but the URL appears absent, and the real-world UQA dataset is proprietary.

Some baseline comparisons are hard to fully assess. Different methods may receive different forms of adaptation, compression, or fine-tuning, and the fairness of comparing memory budgets across token-level, activation-level, and recurrent methods is not completely resolved.

The SCROLLS gains, while positive, are not uniformly dominant. CoMeT trails full-attention fine-tuning overall and underperforms some baselines on several QA/NLI subtasks, so the evidence is stronger for efficient summarization and retrieval than for broad long-context understanding.

The real-world agent evaluation is intriguing but thin: only one main score is reported, comparisons to other efficient methods are absent due to training constraints, and details of task distribution, variance, and statistical reliability are limited.

The layer-level pipeline parallelism contribution is practically useful, but the manuscript gives limited implementation detail and analysis beyond the reported speedup, making it difficult to judge generality across model sizes and systems.

The method is partly incremental relative to prior recurrent-memory Transformers; the main novelty is a well-engineered combination of gated global memory, temporary memory, and training parallelism rather than a clearly new theoretical mechanism.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and highly relevant NLP systems problem: extending pretrained Transformer LLMs to very long contexts with bounded memory and efficient decoding.

The proposed dual-memory design is technically sensible: a gated global memory addresses long-term retention while the FIFO temporary memory preserves recent fine-grained information. The ablations support this decomposition, especially the collapse without gating on the passkey task and the temporary-memory sensitivity on SCROLLS.

The empirical evaluation is fairly broad for a long-context architecture paper, covering SCROLLS, short-context QA, passkey retrieval to 1M tokens, multiple model families/scales, efficiency measurements, and some application-oriented settings.
Efficiency claims are supported by latency and VRAM measurements showing constant decode memory and stable per-token decoding latency, which is a meaningful practical advantage over full attention.
The method appears parameter-efficient and plausibly plug-in for pretrained LLMs, which increases its practical relevance compared with architectures requiring training from scratch.
weaknesses: The main accuracy gains over strong simple baselines are sometimes modest. On SCROLLS, CoMeT improves over sliding-window attention but remains below fine-tuned full attention on the overall average and underperforms it on several QA/NLI tasks, so the broad claim of full-attention-like performance needs narrowing.

The strongest extrapolation result is passkey retrieval, but the model is explicitly fine-tuned on that synthetic task. This supports memory retention under controlled conditions, but it is weak evidence for general arbitrary-length reasoning or retrieval over realistic heterogeneous documents.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript states that code is available but the URL appears missing, and key real-world datasets are proprietary or expert-curated, making the UQA and agent-task results difficult to verify independently.

Some comparisons are not fully controlled. The Terminal-Bench experiment changes model size and context/training setup, excludes most efficient baselines, and reports only a single aggregate number, so it is hard to isolate the contribution of CoMeT from model and setup differences.

The layer-level pipeline parallelism is interesting but under-evaluated: the paper gives a 2.7x speedup claim and visual bubble diagrams, but lacks enough detailed throughput, scaling, hardware utilization, and communication-overhead analysis to fully substantiate the systems contribution.

Several claims are overstated, especially “arbitrarily long” processing and “proven real-world utility.” A fixed-size recurrent memory necessarily has an information bottleneck, and the paper’s own failure analysis shows losses in granularity, causal relations, and long-range aggregation.

The evaluation would be stronger with statistical significance or variance across runs, more realistic long-context benchmarks beyond SCROLLS subsets and passkey retrieval, and deeper comparisons against recent recurrent/linear models under matched hardware and training budgets.

strengths: The paper targets an important and relevant NLP problem: making Transformer-based LLMs usable on very long contexts with bounded memory and practical inference costs.

The proposed architecture is clearly motivated and mostly understandable: the distinction between gated global memory and FIFO temporary memory is intuitive, and the paper provides equations, diagrams, and several ablations that support the role of each component.
The empirical section is broad, covering SCROLLS, shorter QA tasks, synthetic passkey retrieval, efficiency measurements, model-family transfer, and some application-oriented tasks.

The efficiency claims are plausible in direction: chunk-wise recurrent memory should give linear prefill and constant-size retained state, and the reported latency/memory curves are consistent with that design.
The ablations on memory allocation, gating, and RLA rank are useful and help distinguish the contribution from a simple sliding-window or recurrent-cache baseline.
weaknesses: The central claims are overstated relative to the evidence. The paper repeatedly claims arbitrarily long or 1M-token capability, but the strongest support is a synthetic passkey retrieval task with highly artificial repeated distractor text. This does not establish robust long-context reasoning or retention under realistic information density.

Reproducibility is a major concern. The abstract says code is available but no URL is provided. Important application results rely on a proprietary UQA dataset, an LLM-as-judge setup, and expert-generated agent trajectories with insufficient details for independent verification.

The comparison protocol is not fully convincing. Training-free compression baselines are evaluated on the fine-tuned full-attention model, while other baselines are fine-tuned under a unified recipe, but the paper does not sufficiently justify whether this gives each method its best reasonable setting. Several strong recent long-context baselines are discussed but not evaluated.

The novelty is moderate rather than strong. Gated recurrent memory, memory tokens, compression/readout tokens, Transformer-XL-style recurrence, and FIFO/temporary memories are all closely related to prior work. The paper needs a sharper analysis of what is technically new beyond combining these ingredients.

The main benchmark gains are mixed. On SCROLLS, CoMeT improves over efficient baselines on average, but it remains below fine-tuned full attention overall and has notable drops on Qasper, QuALITY, and ContractNLI. The paper emphasizes summarization successes while under-discussing these weaknesses.

The real-world evaluation is under-specified and not very probative. Terminal-Bench uses a different 8B backbone, only compares to full attention, and excludes other efficient methods due to training difficulty. This makes it hard to attribute gains or efficiency to the proposed method rather than setup differences.

The paper lacks statistical rigor. There are no confidence intervals, variance over runs, significance tests, or clear decoding/evaluation stability checks, despite reporting many close differences across methods.

The layer-level pipeline parallelism is potentially useful but not evaluated in enough detail. The claimed 2.7x training speedup lacks a thorough breakdown, comparison across sequence lengths/model sizes, implementation details, and reproducibility guidance.

Some claims are imprecise or misleading. Fixed-size memory gives bounded state, but not necessarily the ability to preserve arbitrary information over arbitrary lengths; the information-theoretic critique of compression methods is also too sweeping given that CoMeT itself compresses history into finite state.

Overall, the work may be a plausible Findings paper after substantial clarification and stronger reproducibility support, but in its current form I would not recommend acceptance because the evidence does not adequately support the breadth of the claims.

strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP systems problem: adapting pretrained Transformer LLMs to much longer contexts with bounded memory. The proposed CoMeT design is technically sensible, combining a gated global recurrent state with FIFO temporary memory for recent detail, and the method is described clearly enough to understand the architectural changes.

The empirical package is broad and mostly convincing: SCROLLS, shorter QA, passkey retrieval up to 1M tokens, efficiency measurements, cross-backbone experiments, hyperparameter ablations, and failure-case analysis. These results support the central claim that the method is a sound and practical efficient long-context module.

The efficiency evidence is a major strength. The reported constant memory, stable decoding latency, and linear prefill scaling are well aligned with the architecture, and the comparison to full attention makes the practical motivation clear.

The ablations are useful: separating global vs temporary memory and removing the gate directly tests key design choices. The passkey ablations in particular support the claim that gated global memory is important for long-range retention.
The paper is generally clear and relevant to ACL/NLP, with a well-motivated connection to long-document processing, QA, summarization, and agent trajectories.
weaknesses: The main 1M-token evidence is mostly based on passkey retrieval, which is a narrow synthetic task. The paper sometimes phrases this as arbitrary long-context processing, but the realistic long-context results are more modest and do not establish robust reasoning or aggregation over million-token inputs.

On SCROLLS, CoMeT is the strongest efficient method on average, but it still trails fine-tuned full attention overall and underperforms it on several QA/NLI-style tasks. The gains are concentrated in summarization and efficiency rather than uniformly better long-context understanding.

The novelty is solid but somewhat incremental: gated recurrent states, memory tokens, FIFO/recent memory, and low-rank adapters all have close precedents. The contribution is mainly a well-engineered combination plus training/inference evidence, not a fundamentally new modeling principle.

Reproducibility has gaps. Some real-world benchmarks appear proprietary or underspecified, the code link is not clearly available in the manuscript text, and implementation details for layer-level pipeline parallelism may be difficult to reproduce despite the appendix.

The comparison set is broad but not always fully satisfying. Some baselines are training-free while others are fine-tuned, the efficient-method training parity is not always easy to verify, and the Terminal-Bench comparison uses different model scale/context settings, making conclusions about general superiority less clean.
The paper lacks uncertainty estimates or statistical significance analysis, which matters because several benchmark differences are relatively small.
